what_it_does: Distributed quantum computing requires sending reliable quantum information between separate quantum processors, but quantum signals degrade rapidly over any physical link. The standard fix is 'entanglement distillation': start with many noisy pairs of entangled qubits shared across a link, then use local operations and classical communication to distill a smaller number of high-quality pairs. The problem is that existing distillation methods either succeed at high quality but waste almost all the raw pairs (very low rate), or preserve more pairs but cannot tolerate the level of noise present in real hardware. This paper presents a new protocol that achieves a 'constant rate' — meaning a fixed fraction of raw pairs always survives as high-fidelity pairs, regardless of how many you start with — by running multiple rounds of distillation using quantum error-detecting codes (codes that flag but do not necessarily fix errors) with progressively increasing efficiency. Numerical optimization is used to tune the protocol for realistic noise levels and finite qubit memory constraints.
